title: I am among you as one who serves (Luke 22:24–38)
hook: at the table they argue who's greatest, and he tells Peter: I prayed for you

segments.voice: Yesterday, anamnesis: remembrance that brings the past into the present, at a table Jesus longed for. Your line: I have longed for this.

The room might have gone silent. Jesus has just given them bread and said it's his body. He's just said one of them will betray him. And what happens next, Luke tells us without softening it, is an argument. Over dinner. About which of them is the greatest. It's almost funny, and painfully familiar: the meeting where everyone angles for credit, the family dinner where old rankings come back out. The friends at this table are doing exactly what people do.

Jesus doesn't shout. He asks a question. Kings lord it over people, he says, and get called benefactors. Not so with you. Then, in the King James words: "For whether is greater, he that sitteth at meat, or he that serveth? is not he that sitteth at meat? but I am among you as he that serveth." Everyone knows the answer: the one at the table outranks the one carrying the plates. And Jesus says, I'm the one carrying the plates. The Greek word for serving is the root of the word deacon. Then he turns to Peter, and his voice changes. "Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat." The King James keeps a detail modern English can't show: in the Greek, that first you is plural. All of you will be shaken like grain in a sieve. Then the next line goes singular, just to Peter: "But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren." Peter protests that he's ready to go to prison and to death. Jesus tells him that before the rooster crows today, he will deny three times that he knows him. Hear the order. The prayer comes before the failure. Jesus already knows Peter will fall, he has already prayed, and he's already given him a job for afterward: when you've come back, strengthen the others.
screen: `KINGS LORD IT; NOT SO WITH YOU.`
`I PRAYED FOR YOU, BEFORE YOU FELL.`
then, large: `I HAVE PRAYED FOR THEE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone heading into something hard, a test, a recovery, a marriage under strain, someone who might not make it through cleanly, and don't rehearse their mistakes. If you pray, do what Jesus did: pray for them now, ahead of time, that their faith won't fail. If you don't, hold them in good will, and decide now how you'll treat them if they stumble.
Deacon. The word rooted in Jesus's claim that at his table, he is the one who serves, carrying the plates instead of sitting to be served.
Your line: I have prayed for you. First the prayer, then the fall, then the way back. Until next time.

howItsDone: Churches that have deacons take the title from the same family of Greek words Jesus uses here for serving, and Christians pray for one another by name, especially for people facing a hard test.

fork.setup: Peter has just promised to go with Jesus to prison and to death. Jesus knows he will deny him three times tonight. what does Jesus say to him?
options: tell him to leave before he fails.
tell him you've prayed for him, and to strengthen the others afterward.
say nothing and let it happen.
fork.reveal: "I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren." the prayer and the job come before the fall.

original.note: Greek: the one who serves, who waits at table. from the same root as the word deacon.

trapdoor: what you thought: be humble, and pray for your friends.
what it means: at Jesus's table the greatest serves, and he prays for Peter before Peter fails, then gives him work for afterward.
what a scholar hears: in 22:31 'you' is plural (all of them sifted) and in 22:32 'thee' is singular; the King James keeps the difference that modern 'you' can't show.
recall: the one near you, a neighbor
guess: a church servant, from the Greek word for serving
the head of a church, ranked above the priests
a monk who lives apart in prayer and silence

chat.says: Why do churches call some of their helpers deacons? Where does the word come from?
options: From the Greek for serving: Jesus said, I am among you as he that serveth.
From a Greek title for the disciple who sat nearest to Jesus at supper.
From the Greek for elder: the oldest disciples were put in charge of meals.
chat.meaning: Jesus asks who is greater, the one at the table or the one who serves, and says: I am among you as he that serveth.

benefactors.meaning: a title rulers liked: people who do good for others

sift you as wheat.meaning: shake you hard, like grain tossed in a sieve

brethren.meaning: an old word for brothers; here, the other disciples

Deacon.meaning: a church servant; the word comes from the Greek for serving
